An estimation of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time for $B^0_s$ mesons has been made with the help of around 37 picobarns of LHCb data from 2010. This measure allows for constraints on theories beyond the Standard Model that may influence the $B^0_s$ system and was found to be 1.440 picoseconds by employing two methods with varying degrees of uncertainty, specifically 0.096 (statistical) ± 0.008 (systematic) ± 0.003 (model-based).

This research paper focuses on the numerical solution of a stochastic control problem governed by a parabolic equation with the control variable affecting the diffusion coefficient, particularly with the presence of rough inputs; it establishes the convergence of a specific numerical discretization method and provides an alternative solution using a stochastic simulation technique known as the Monte-Carlo method.

Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. These anisotropy signals are evident in the most energetic cosmic rays with powers of 8 to 12 EeV and principal components of full sky directions (θ,φ). The most likely explanations for these anisotropy patterns are either cosmic ray sources or interference patterns created during the journey of cosmic rays. If the anisotropy is attributed to source patterns, various assumptions about the distribution of sources and their radiation patterns enable the estimation of source densities. The most plausible model suggests that the density of sources is extremely high, with 10^10 to 10^11 cosmic ray producers located within the nearest billion light-years. Alternatively, if the anisotropy is the result of interference patterns, the most likely scenario involves the 180-degree phase shift between two aligned waves, suggesting that the most energetic cosmic rays originate from a relatively small, narrowly focused beam with a diameter of approximately 8 million light years.
This paper proves that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over a given field possesses a specific characteristic - nilpotency, building on a previous discovery that these algebras are solvable.

This study provides first-time data on the fluctuations of particle angles and magnitudes in proton-proton collisions at a 13 TeV energy level, significantly expanding the previous research. A 2018 paper by the same authors established first observations of angle and magnitude fluctuations in lower-energy collisions. The current research extends this finding to higher energies, where it reveals similar trends and characteristics. It achieves this through the application of four-dimensional cumulative distribution functions, taking into consideration the inherent spread of such fluctuations. The study also compares its findings with existing theoretical models, highlighting discrepancies and areas for future theoretical development.

This research develops a statistical framework for processing tables that contain inaccuracies and discrepancies, with the goal of creating a robust and adaptable method for handling various types of data quality issues, including missing and erroneous entries, inconsistencies, and inaccuracies in numerical values. The proposed approach utilizes a distribution called the 'Mixture of Distributions' to represent each entry in the table, allowing it to effectively handle data quality problems by switching between different distributions. Furthermore, the development of a robust and adaptable method for processing tables with data quality issues is made possible by the incorporation of hyper-priors and hyper-processes from the 'Hierarchical Bayes' framework. The performance and applicability of the proposed approach are demonstrated through computational experiments and real-world applications, including the analysis of a dataset with entry-level errors and the comparison of numeric values in two tables from the 'Housing Prices' dataset.

This study presents a novel dynamic econometric model called Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with external covariates, specifically designed to analyze and forecast count-based time series data. Our research indicates that a score-driven approach is particularly effective in capturing the evolution of time-varying parameters and allows for modeling complex dynamics and shifts within such data sets. Furthermore, we have analyzed the theoretical characteristics of the TV-PARX model, demonstrating under mild conditions that maximum likelihood estimation yields reliable and normally-distributed estimates of model parameters. To evaluate the TV-PARX model's performance and forecasting capabilities in real-world scenarios, we conducted a series of Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, we have applied the time-varying specification of the TV-PARX model to empirical data sets, analyzing new daily COVID-19 cases in Italy and corporate defaults in the US.

We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
category-level descriptors. We apply this representation in object manipulation,
with the aim of repeating tasks on new object instances from the same category
after witnessing a single demonstration. To achieve this, we use optimization
to locate the pose whose descriptor corresponds to that in the demonstration. NDFs
are efficiently trained without expert input, using only categorical data and
self-supervised pose variation. When compared to competitors, our approach
demonstrates improved performance in both 2D and 3D scenarios. The code for NDFs is
available at: https://github.com/robotics-agents/ndf.

Using the functional renormalization group at the next-to-leading order in the derivative expansion, we have updated the position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity for O(N) universality classes in classic scenarios. Specifically for QCD's relevant universality classes in three dimensions, we have determined $|z_c|/R_\chi^{1/\gamma}$ to be approximately 1.607, 1.589 for $N=2, 4$ respectively. Alternatively, we have also determined the scaling behavior of the Yang-Lee edge singularity near $N=4$, finding that the shift in $z_c$ follows $z_c \approx 4.762 R_\chi^{1/\gamma}$ for $0.001\lesssim R_\chi\lesssim 10^{-4}$, and the associated critical exponent displays a regular 1/R_\chi variation across this range.

In statistics and machine learning, it is frequently essential to establish whether a basic optimization method on a non-convex function can eventually enter a region where the function becomes locally convex. To address this, we developed an inequality that enables us to analyze the properties of the optimization landscape surrounding the solutions produced by an approximate message passing (AMP) algorithm. Specifically, we applied our inequality to demonstrate the local convexity of a particular TAP free energy function, which is relevant to the Z2 synchronization problem and the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model. Additionally, our inequality led to a confirmation of a previous conjecture regarding the efficiency of a sampling algorithm in the low temperature regime.

While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving a precision of 0.01 for measuring the aerosol depth has been challenging. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a by-product. Our team used extensive data from the FRAM camera at the Pierre Auger Observatory and a similar camera at the VLT to discover that systematic errors are the main precision issue. These errors are likely caused by inconsistent calibration procedures and varying field-of-view measurements. We successfully applied a calibration-independent approach that uses the altitude distribution of the measurements and validated the method by comparing the calculated and actual values. By solving the issues with the detector calibration, we achieved an accuracy of 0.012 for the aerosol depth measurements.

Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main groups based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of quaternion coordinates in the pose estimation task. Our research focuses on enhancing two-stage pipelines by introducing a new approach to predict object-centered coordinates. An initial estimate for this prediction is generated via a proposal-based method, and the remaining estimates are obtained through refinement using a CNN. Our suggested approach, along with current proposal-based methods and two-stage pipelines, is demonstrated through experimental results and evaluations. Our findings indicate that the proposed approach yields comparable performance to existing solutions.

We present GGLasso, a Python library designed to address General Graphical Lasso
challenges. Based on the original work of Friedman (2007), Graphical Lasso
estimates a sparsely constructed inverse covariance matrix $\Theta$ from
multivariate Gaussian data $\mathcal{X}$, initially introduced by Dempster (1972)
under Covariance Selection. The framework has been expanded to accommodate
hidden variables in Chandrasekaran (2012) and can jointly estimate multiple
inverse covariance matrices, as shown in Danaher (2013) and Tomasi (2018). The
GGLasso package supports the resolution of diverse formulations and notable
subcases like Graphical Lasso with latent variables, Group, and Fused Graphical Lasso.

Numerous numerical methods for resolving stochastic differential equations in molecular dynamics simulations have been scrutinized and assessed, focusing on deterministic impulses, drifts, and Brownian motions. By utilizing the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion, recent studies found that the methods' accuracy could be evaluated in terms of the impact of the step size on configurational averaging. Results showed that for harmonic oscillators, some methods yield precise configurational averages, potentially leading to better performance in biomolecular simulations, especially in cases where bond stretches play a crucial role. Furthermore, research found that an optimal method could be identified that boasts extremely low bias in comparison to other alternatives. Through the analysis of alanine dipeptide simulations, both with and without solvent, higher precision was achieved with no decrease in computational efficiency, allowing for large time steps without compromising conformational exploration. Ultimately, the most efficient method demonstrated enhanced molecular sampling, yielding overall improvements of at least 25% in feasible time steps in vacuum and reductions of at least a factor of ten in configurational average errors in solvent simulations with larger time steps.

Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks that incorporate node importance across different layers. In these networks, defined by separate interconnected graphs without connections between different layers, the value of a node's centrality is determined by the sum of the values of the connected nodes within each specific layer, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality calculations. Unlike standard approaches, our approach takes into account the relationships between different network layers and their respective impact on the centrality values. Unlike current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks that account for inter-layer connections, our approach uses a separate set of equations that can be solved using a hybrid algorithm.

Recently, we generated the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra using deformed Poisson brackets, 
which contain an $f$-parameter and are defined within de Sitter spacetime. Now, 
we employ the same approach to derive the same algebra within this same spacetime 
framework, but with an $f$-parameter set to zero. Consequently, we obtained the same 
equations of motion as previously calculated. Additionally, we determined the wave 
equations that correspond to the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra within this same spacetime 
setting, but with the $f$-parameter equated to a specific value.

This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. In fact, at mid-range speeds, pinch-off times relate differently to fluid dynamics than they do at either low or high speeds, indicating that increased pressures inside the formed cavity play a significant role. In addition, our findings include the shift from the deeper water-entrapment phenomenon to the surface-seal regime, and observations on the partial-seal, rippling-cavity-surface, and secondary pinch-off stages of water-entry interactions.

A well-known hypothesis posits that gravity at a quantum level must be devoid of universal symmetries. We studied an array of Type IIB $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories to investigate the possibility of universal symmetries in the context of a non-vanishing three-form antisymmetric tensor field. Our analysis revealed that a class of $\theta$-terms, which can arise as generalized $\theta$-terms after a consistent reduction scheme, lead to the violation of global symmetries. However, we established that the effects of these $\theta$-terms on the vacuum expectation value of the dilaton field are marginal within the low-energy expansion framework. Moreover, our findings indicated that the violation of global symmetries is a universal phenomenon in string theory, arising from the interaction between the three-form $\theta$-terms and the dilaton field.

Our calculations using first-principles methods reveal that cubanite exhibits unusual orbital selectivity, with electrons occupying certain molecular orbitals while being localized in other atomic ones. This phenomenon is exceptionally rare in 3d transition metal compounds, providing a theoretical basis for the experimentally observed lack of charge disproportionation, anomalous Mössbauer spectra, and ferromagnetic coupling between adjacent iron ions.

A burgeoning field in quantum physics, known as multi-phonon physics, is driving research and development for both fundamental understanding and applications in metrology and communication systems. Quantum acoustic resonators serve as the ideal testing ground for multi-phonon phenomena through both theoretical and experimental studies. Excitons in a semiconductor quantum well or dot have proven to be highly effective for detecting even a single phonon due to their extreme sensitivity. However, because of their short lifetimes and scattering off photons, dark excitons exhibit significantly lower reactivity compared to bright excitons. Consequently, dark excitons might be more suitable for precise multi-phonon measurements by minimizing unwanted interactions and prolonging their lifespan. This research computationally investigates the interaction between a Michelson-type quantum acoustic cavity and both bright and dark excitons within a GaAs quantum dot. It also determines the conditions under which phonon-photon-exciton correlations occur and the validity of the effective mass approximation in this scenario.

Our investigation focuses on a 2D electronic lattice from a non-symmorphic wallpaper group.  We're examining a herringbone lattice with two types of glide symmetries in perpendicular directions using a nearest-neighbor tight-binding model. This model contains horizontal and vertical hopping terms and reveals two distinct non-equivalent Dirac cones within the first Brillouin zone along a high-symmetry path. These cones can be modified through various perturbations of the Hamiltonian. These perturbations disrupt the lattice symmetries by applying differing onsite potentials at the lattice sites, which causes the Dirac cones to collapse into semi-Dirac cones and nodal lines along the high-symmetry paths. Additionally, we observed topological characteristics through the calculation of the Berry curvature and the topological charge of the semi-Dirac points.

Quantum states known as single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated via quantum-optical catalysis using beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. These states occur when a coherent state and a single-photon state interact in two input ports, and a photon is detected in a specific output channel. We examine the success probabilities associated with identifying these states, as they depend on the number of photons transmitted and the transmission coefficient of the beam splitter. Our analysis is supplemented by simulations of actual quantum experiments using both continuous-variable Thomas-Reidler states and discrete-variable number states, in addition to calculating various quantum properties of SPCCSs, including their entanglement, von Neumann entropy, and Wigner function dynamics.

In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the use of bivectors plays a key role in identifying the precise solutions to Einstein's field equations. This review focuses on explaining the fundamental principles and detailed calculations of bivectors within the Newman-Penrose formalism, specifically by converting a complex self-dual electromagnetic field from the standard Minkowski space basis to the complex null tetrad basis. As a result, we derive the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor in the context of Newman-Penrose formalism.

A recent framework combining artificial neural networks and mixed integer linear programming for designing chemical compounds has been built upon to create a new method for polymer inference. This new method incorporates a unique way of depicting polymers using monomers, new descriptors that capture their structure, and employs linear regression in the predictive framework. Computational trials have demonstrated that the proposed approach excels in predicting specific chemical properties in polymers, also successfully modeling compounds composed of up to 50 non-hydrogen atoms within a monomeric structure.

Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other medical imaging techniques, medical histories, or clinical data related to laboratory tests. Acquiring and utilizing this additional information often results in increased treatment planning time and costs. To streamline treatment planning and minimize costs, this study proposes using a deep learning system that only relies on CT scans for tumor identification, thereby obviating the need for supplementary information. Our proposed system consists of two components: a primary model that locates the start and end points of the tumor along the entire esophagus based on CT scans, and a secondary model that outlines the exact boundaries of the tumor. Our system has achieved high accuracy in tumor segmentation and could serve as a valuable tool for pre-surgical preparation.

Multilingual individuals possess a high level of proficiency in two or more languages, enabling effective written and oral communication across multiple languages. When communicating, they may blend languages, also known as code-switching or code-mixing, by switching between different languages within a single utterance. This research explores current NLP developments, constraints, and potential obstacles in tackling five critical issues affecting multilingual communities: crisis management, healthcare, election campaigns, fake news dissemination, and hate speech. To move forward, we outline potential future datasets, models, and resources to enhance NLP applications for societal betterment, exemplified through an analysis of code-mixing between English and Hindi but with implications for other language combinations.

Human-generated descriptions are commonly used to train and evaluate image description systems, which are typically ranked based on their similarity to these descriptions. This method's reliability hinges on the quality of these descriptions. Since, as demonstrated in Section 2, current datasets are inadequate, I believe we require more precise guidelines balancing visually impaired users' needs and practical description generation feasibility. High-quality reference data could be ideal for system evaluation, yet we should also consider other alternatives.

Tantalum oxide compounds, with the formula Ta$_2$O$_5$, are distinguished by unique properties including high dielectric values and minimal reflectivity. Recent studies have also considered Ta$_2$O$_5$ as materials that can detect spinal fluid, a bodily fluid found in the brain. To further understand the behavior of Ta$_2$O$_5$, researchers have used advanced computational methods to simulate the interactions of electrons within Ta$_2$O$_5$ using gradient-corrected density functional theory. Evaluations have shown that Ta$_2$O$_5$ has the ability to absorb protons, making it a promising material for cancer treatment. Evaluations have also allowed for the visualization of Ta$_2$O$_5$'s spatial distribution within the brain.

Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation was more widely shared in states with larger populations having similar social views and found this effect to be two times greater than the influence of factors like a user's trust in news sources and personality traits like conscientiousness. We also showed that users were more likely to share misinformation with users who held similar political views and that this behavior was more prevalent in states with greater social segregation. We used an agent-based model to explain these findings and highlight potential implications for news source effectiveness in such divided environments.

Humans employ spoken language to efficiently teach other people various skills. Although robotic demonstrations are a natural teaching method, learning from solely observed actions does not take full advantage of audio feedback from the instructor, which is typically available and carries significant meaning and value. To effectively utilize audio during teaching, it's essential to understand the content being conveyed. This study examines how audio features related to task instructions, feedback, and comments affect the ability of a robot to perform a task after a demonstration involving speech and action. The results indicate that audio significantly enhances the robot's performance and that the robot can prioritize audio over visual cues when demonstrations involve conflicting information. Additionally, the robot's performance is improved when there is consistent audio feedback for certain task conditions, but it may be hindered by contradictory audio. The findings also show that the robot's ability to perform tasks successfully increases with the quality of the speech it is trained to recognize.

Quantum field theory complexity is particularly hard to define, especially when transitioning beyond simple free models and their corresponding Gaussian representations. A promising approach to address this challenge is through the study of conformal field theories in 1+1 dimensions, specifically focusing on the universal sector of the energy-momentum tensor in this context. A key unifying framework consists of Euler-Arnold equations and their broader integro-differential generalizations, which provide a framework for calculating action-minimizing complexity for the state, as well as related operator complexity metrics. Notably, this approach has been effectively applied to the study of the tricritical Ising model by utilizing the known properties of the toroidal CFT. Moreover, the framework has been shown to yield consistent results across different normalization conventions. Additionally, the study of the tricritical Ising model model highlights the importance of accounting for the normalizable zero-mode of the stress tensor, which gives rise to a constant contribution to the complexity. The issue with this mode can be resolved by either fixing the mode explicitly or introducing an additional term to the defining integro-differential operator. The latter approach is analogous to the practice of renormalizing the zero-mode in the context of the thermal entropy.

Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Although they have achieved considerable success, interactions with these systems often rely on a linear sequence of inputs and outputs, lacking the depth that characterizes human conversation. To truly emulate the essence of conversations, knowledge about the participants, their shared background, and the context is essential, a concept that has been demonstrated through natural spoken interactions but remains challenging to automate. To tackle this issue, researchers have been using artificial intelligence algorithms, but with limited effectiveness, primarily due to the lack of large-scale, high-quality data necessary for training and evaluating these systems. To address this challenge, this work introduces a novel approach, the Contextual Conversational Graph, which leverages knowledge graphs to incorporate background information and employs graph neural networks to capture contextual aspects, ultimately generating responses that are informed by the context. Moreover, this work develops a metric to evaluate the contextual understanding of conversations, in addition to utilizing existing metrics to assess the generated responses' coherence and relevance. Experimental evaluations have shown that the proposed system and metric outperform existing approaches in multiple assessments.

Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across each data-poor domain. The empirical evaluations on real-world datasets unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-target and dual-target CDR approaches and the effectiveness of its components.

Convex optimization issues often take on a more manageable form when represented with conic formulations that leverage a wide variety of exotic cones. Exotic cones in this context, refer to specialized geometric shapes with properties enabling efficient implementation of computational tools, specifically barrier oracles for their own and dual shapes. This work introduces Hypatia, an interior-point solver designed to handle these complex shapes with ease. Developed using Julia and interfacing with JuMP, Hypatia can utilize pre-specified descriptions of these cones to solve various optimization problems efficiently. It also features the ability to convert well-known standard cones, such as the second-order cone, to the exotic format, enabling comparisons of its performance. Hypatia's capabilities are demonstrated through benchmark tests of common exotic cones, including 3-dimensional Lorentz cones, the hyperbolic cone, the rotated cone, the powersum cone, the cone of complex loresntz vectors, and standard cones.

The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality control to reduce labor costs and minimize errors. Our investigation focuses on a subset of MRI analysis tasks, specifically those relying on machine learning models, where our quality control framework aims to enhance performance by integrating data filtering techniques. We tested our proposed system for automated quality control among three MRI-based analysis applications, analyzing the results to determine factors influencing its effectiveness. The findings showed our quality control system effectively enhanced the accuracy of machine learning models for MRI analysis. Our research revealed that employing data filtering methods that consider both image quality and anatomical content can produce more notable improvements in low-quality data analysis compared to high-quality data analysis. Our quality control framework further demonstrated analytical scalability, exhibiting no decrease in performance with increased training datasets. Our study identified the optimal filter settings that balance the trade-off between precision and recall, which in turn influence the effectiveness of automated quality control. Our investigation provides a framework for automated quality control that can be applied to other MRI-based analysis tasks, with implications for improving model generalizability when training on low-quality datasets.

To understand how private electric vehicles influence the recovery of power grids following outages, we developed a mathematical framework that incorporates decentralized decision-making in both transportation and energy systems. We utilized multi-agent optimization to model this process and overcame computational challenges through an efficient algorithm based on precise reformation. Numerical analysis was conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, yielding valuable policy insights and paving the way for further study into grid resilience with private EVs within interconnected transportation and energy networks.

The Motivation Dynamics framework, a concept explored in recent studies that applies bifurcations to model an autonomous agent's decision-making processes, is further developed to accommodate multiple autonomous entities in this paper. We demonstrate how the framework's capabilities can be expanded to capture persistent, cooperative behavior between agents meeting at specific locations, and through in-depth analysis and numerical data, reveal that this extension exhibits a complex pattern indicative of a strange attractor.

This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 ($x = 0.25$, $0.5$, and $0.75$) using a full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the generalized gradient approximation+U. We studied the fundamental properties of bulk GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 materials crystallizing in the AuCu3 structure. Our results match previous experimental and theoretical data on the GdSn3 compound and indicate that CmSn3 and GdSn3 both adopt a type-A anti-ferromagnetic configuration and display metallic behavior. Notably, the magnetic moment diminishes with rising Cm content in the GdxCm1-xSn3 series, yet remains in the 0.7-1.0 $\mu$B range for all compositions examined.

The paper reviews predictions made by an extension of the standard model called the bilepton model, which involves changing the fundamental symmetry group from $SU(2) \times U(1)$ to $SU(3)\times U(1)$, while assigning the three fermion families in a non-consecutive manner. For consistency, three fermion families are necessary as indicated by triangle anomaly cancellation and asymptotic freedom. In the bilepton model, novel physical phenomena are predicted to occur, including bileptons and three types of heavy quarks: ${\cal D}$, ${\cal S}$, and ${\cal T}$. Theoretical calculations suggest that Quantum Chromodynamics will result in heavy quarks bonding to each other or light quarks to form composite particles like baryons and mesons that might be detectable with a next-generation 100 TeV particle accelerator but are too heavy for the current LHC.

The concept of ordered generating sequences (OGS) extends a fundamental property of finite abelian groups to non-abelian groups, providing a distinct generalization. According to its definition, any element within a group can be expressed as a product of various generator powers, arranged in a specific order. For the symmetric group Sn, R. Shwartz established a significant finding by proving that every permutation within the group Sn can be generated using a specific sequence of the following operations: (i) taking a power of an existing generator, (ii) replacing a generator with another one, or (iii) swapping two generators. Our research builds upon this discovery and demonstrates that for the Coxeter group G(B), which encompasses the symmetric group Sn as a specific case, we can derive an ordered generating sequence (OGS) for the group G(B) based on the matrix B that defines the group. Our results also apply to the braid groups B_nN), the Artin group (B_n), and the Hecke reflection groups H_n).

Utilizing the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and Sloan Digital Sky Survey, we've developed a method to calculate weak lensing convergence by combining data on the positions and photometry of foreground galaxies. A correlation between this approach and the residual Hubble diagram values of Type Ia supernovae holds a $3.6\sigma$ significance and is consistent with dark matter effects due to galactic halos. Furthermore, we constrained galactic halo properties, including the mass-to-light ratio $\gamma$ and the radial distribution of matter density within haloes $\rho(r)$. Based on this analysis, we formulated an equation to calculate the lens-induced additional random scattering in SN Ia magnitudes as $\sigma_{\rm lens} = (0.06 \pm 0.017) \cdot (d_{\rm c} / d_{\rm ob})$. As a result, the net observed SN Ia magnitude becomes a combination of intrinsic SN Ia brightness, the distance to the object, and the effects of lensing, in addition to a random scattering component. We also found that this scattering component could account for $3.4\sigma$ of the observed tension between SN Ia absolute magnitudes and Hubble diagram slopes when considering intrinsic SN Ia properties alone. Given this finding, we propose an adjustment to the standard SN Ia Hubble diagram analysis that incorporates lensing-induced scattering, which may provide a more accurate interpretation of existing SN Ia datasets and those to

The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic spins with an addressable frequency. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure the electronic spin resonance with a million-fold increase in sensitivity, we were able to investigate the magnetic properties of T centers within the 10 nm surface layer of the device layer. Our findings indicate that surface T centers exhibit reduced spin lifetimes and frequency ranges compared to buried T centers. Nonetheless, we have successfully demonstrated the operation of a single-photon device that interfaces with electronic spins, using a buried T-type defect center integrated within the 220nm device layer of an SOI platform.

For our task that considers context, a suitable object detector is needed.
Different object detectors exploit scene context for recognition in varying ways.
This study categorizes object detectors into 3 groups based on context usage:
one that doesn't use context by isolating the input, another that uses partial
context by isolating part of the feature map, and one that uses full context
without isolation.
Our evaluation method assesses the effect of context for each deep detector
category systematically. A specially designed dataset is created to test the
effect of context for deep detectors. The impact of removing the background
context and foreground objects on the MS COCO is also examined.
It is shown that both two-stage and single-stage object detectors can make use
of the context due to their extensive receptive field.
Thus, selecting the best object detector for a particular application depends
on the specific context in question.

The main objective of this paper is to investigate multiple solution possibilities for a specific Kirchhoff type elliptic system of equations that are given by the system of equations where $m\left(\sum^k_{j=1}\|u_j\|^2\right)\Delta u_i=\frac{f_i(x,u_1,\ldots,u_k)}{|x|^\beta}+\varepsilon h_i(x)$ holds for $i=1,\ldots,k$, within the bounded domain $\Omega$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$, where $x$ contains the origin with smooth boundary, and for a certain condition $\beta\in [0,2)$; here $m$ denotes a function that belongs to Kirchhoff type, $f_i$ behave like $e^{\beta s^2}$, and there is a function $h_i\in \left(\big(H^1_0(\Omega)\big)^*,\|\cdot\|_*\right)$. By making use of a singular Trudinger-Moser inequality for a small positive value $\varepsilon$ and variational methods, we are able to establish sufficient conditions for a multiplicity of the system's solutions given the given conditions.

We examine the concentration behavior of functionals of random vectors whose entries reside in the discrete cube. These vectors must adhere to either the stochastic covering property (SCP) or the strong Rayleigh property (SRP). Our findings concerning SCP measures yield new subgaussian inequalities of a bounded-difference type, while our results related to SRP measures provide tighter inequalities than those currently available. Additionally, we establish that the optimal inequality for a given measure can be obtained by considering a modified version of that measure, which we term the renewal measure associated with the original measure. This association is useful for deriving inequalities for the sums of independent, identically distributed random variables, whose common distribution is linked to the original measure. Our approach is motivated by an analysis of the relationship between the SCP and the renewal measure associated with the renewal process, as described in the works of Feller, Kingman, and others. Our research extends the subgaussian inequalities related to the SCP to include functions of a single variable and matrix-valued functions, thereby expanding the scope of these inequalities.

Wilberd van der Kallen translated this 1951 thesis into English, originally written by T.A. Springer. Springer investigated the method of categorizing conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K), specifically focusing on fields K with a characteristic other than two. His work revealed that each conjugacy class can be distinguished using a combination of invariant characteristics. These characteristics initially mirror those found in the general linear group – namely, irreducible polynomials and systems of non-negative integers – but also incorporate additional properties, such as unique configurations of Hermitian forms and quadratic forms, each belonging to a specific equivalence class.

A key obstacle in kidney transplants arises from the incompatibility between donors and patients, which has been exacerbated by the growing scarcity of kidney donors. Desensitization techniques were developed to overcome the immunological difficulties. Patients receiving incompatible transplants face a higher risk of transplant rejection, infections, and cancer, and are more likely to lose their transplants. We aim to find the optimal acceptance criteria for end-stage kidney patients by potentially receiving incompatible kidneys. A Markov Decision Process model is introduced, which accounts for the level of incompatibility as a key factor, making it a more complex problem to solve, but with suitable conditions, it is possible to establish control limit policies that can be easily applied. Our study uses numerical examples to demonstrate how the optimal policy behaves under different levels of incompatibility, and highlights the significance of taking incompatibility into consideration in decision-making, especially when desensitization treatments are available.

This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora that yield distinct outcomes, thereby shedding light on the conditions under which these models succeed or fail.

This article presents the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based IDET systems as alternatives to our previously proposed optimal wideband waveforming strategy in [1].
Fair-throughput and sum-throughput optimisation problems are defined and formulated.
By leveraging an algorithm that utilizes fixed points, we derive the optimal fair-throughput and sum-throughput values for SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems.

This research introduces a new method to model the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques. By leveraging the strengths of these approaches, we've developed a numerical strategy utilizing Cartesian grids to efficiently handle complex boundary transformations and high-resolution interface representation, thus enabling the simulation of melting and bonding without difficulty. The implementation of a second-order conservative numerical scheme for the conservation equations on an embedded grid structure allows for the exploration of diverse boundary evolution scenarios.

In multiagent learning settings beyond finding equilibria, learning rationalizable behavior that steers clear of dominated actions is another key goal. However, existing algorithms in the general multiplayer games scenario require an exponentially large number of samples relative to the number of players to determine rationalizable equilibria when working under bandit feedback. In an attempt to address this issue, we develop an innovative Coarse Correlated Equilibria learning framework, which yields significantly improved sample efficiency by reducing the required samples to polynomial proportions. To achieve this reduction, our approach involves first obtaining an efficient estimate of the minimal removal depth property, which serves as a key condition for applying our proposed CCE learning algorithm. Moreover, our research showcases that Coarse Correlated Equilibria and Correlated Equilibria converge to the same rationalizable profiles, thereby establishing the theoretical guarantee for our sample-efficient algorithm. Our empirical studies also reveal that our proposed framework excels in practice by yielding more generalizable solutions in various settings.

An analysis of a stochastic Susceptible to Infective to Recovered model is conducted, where the model is based on an Erdős-Rényi random graph that changes dynamically as susceptible individuals connected to infected neighbours form new connections or sever existing ones. As the model is scaled to accommodate large populations, researchers obtained mathematical proofs of key properties of the model, particularly its early stages and the phase where the epidemic spreads rapidly. They also found that under certain conditions, there are sharp thresholds where the model suddenly switches between two completely different behaviours. It has been proven that these transitions are more dramatic if the model is changed to only form new connections to uninfected individuals, where the model suddenly switches from no infections to complete spread.

Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately fitting probability density functions. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since processes are often measured across a wide range of scales, evolution equations such as DGLAP need to be applied to PDF candidates or already precomputed in the outputs, necessitating a unified framework that can automate this process for the benefit of research groups working on PDF fitting and potential phenomenological studies.

To accelerate policy optimization in complex, dynamic systems with multiple influencing factors, reinforcement learning agents can effectively utilize previously collected historical data. Standard experience replay enables agents to retain information from prior iterations. However, the current approach equally values all collected observations, neglecting their varying significance. A more adaptive method, the variance reduction based experience replay framework, selectively leverages the most informative historical data. This approach prioritizes past observations more likely to represent the current target distribution. Theoretical and practical evaluations demonstrate that this method accelerates optimal policy discovery and boosts the effectiveness of state-action values function estimation.

In our analysis of conversational dialogue, we face numerous possible responses 
to any given history, leading us to present the MultiTalk Dataset. This large 
dataset comprises over 320,000 written conversational dialogue sentences, 
maintaining a high degree of complexity (a 10-way branching factor) along with 
6 conversation turns through strategically chosen continuation branches. Our study 
of dialogue generation involves multiple advancements, particularly in highly 
branching scenarios. To evaluate the diversity of generated text, we introduce a 
simple scoring algorithm grounded in bipartite graph matching, enabling efficient 
computation despite high branch factors. Our research spans multiple text 
generation tasks in English, incorporating various models and evaluating their 
performance through the diversity of generated text using the MultiTalk Dataset.

We introduce MG-GLAM, a computational tool developed to rapidly generate simulations of cosmological datasets in modified gravity theories, specifically f(R)-gravity. This program builds upon previous work in modified gravity simulations, including the original GLAM algorithm, and offers several key advantages over existing methods for modeling general relativity in cosmological contexts. Compared to other simulation codes, the current version excels at minimizing the number of parameters required and is highly efficient in its implementation, utilizing an advanced technique to leverage numerical datasets for N-body simulations. Furthermore, this code can simulate the evolution of both dark matter and dark energy within the cosmological context.

Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate that such connections can be made locally by driving multiple SLE with the Dyson model on the real line and the Bru-Wishart process on the positive reals, respectively. Ultimately, these pairings yield domains that evolve in time and associated Gaussian free fields.

MediaWiki's 'WorkingWiki' is an open-source extension that converts a wiki
into a sophisticated collaborative platform for developing high-quality manuscripts
and software projects. Originally developed at McMaster University's theoretical
biology lab, WorkingWiki enables multiple users to work together on a range of
tasks by utilizing command-line tools to translate raw'source code' into desired outputs.
Its features include the ability to write programs in languages such as R, Python,
and C, as well as utilizing tools like GNU Make, Julia, and Mathematica, all within
the wiki interface. By automating tasks like error detection, testing, and formatting,
WorkingWiki facilitates seamless collaboration between its users. This document
provides a step-by-step guide for installing and utilizing the WorkingWiki extension
on any wiki platform.

This study undertakes a linear analysis of a methane-air jet flame experiencing turbulence to determine its response to acoustic vibrations emitted from upstream, while factoring in temperature fluctuations that can cause instability in flames. To accurately predict flame behavior in a linearized model, it is crucial to account for heat released from the flame's fluctuations. Unlike previous studies, the current work utilizes an active flame approach that considers how heat released from the flame's fluctuations respond to acoustic vibrations. To apply this approach in a linear framework, the model must utilize the heat released fluctuations' relationship with the flame's velocity and density fluctuations. To establish this relationship, the work begins with a fundamental expression of the heat released per unit time from the flame, then simplifies it based on assumptions made about the flame's chemistry. The resulting model can be utilized in a linearized model and demonstrates how heat released fluctuations influence the flame's response to acoustic vibrations. Furthermore, the model enables the investigation of how turbulence affects heat released fluctuations and, in turn, how this effect influences the flame's stability. The findings from the model are compared to previous studies that neglected heat released fluctuations. The current work also introduces a new flame time scale that characterizes the flame's response to acoustic vibrations and determines its stability. The model is validated using numerical simulations of the jet flame, which include both laminar and turbulent flow conditions. The introduction of the new flame time scale provides a useful tool for predicting the effects of turbulence and heat released fluctuations on flame stability in jet

We investigate the neutrinoless double beta decay driven by an extremely light dark matter field interacting with neutrinos, particularly focusing on the impact when this interaction breaches the lepton number, which directly leads to a significant influence on the $0\nu \beta \beta$ decay, even when neutrino masses are very small. Since the ultralight dark matter can be adequately modeled as a classical field, this interaction's effect is reflected in a periodic oscillation in the number of decay events. Nevertheless, we find that in the early universe, this interaction would almost certainly disrupt standard cosmological outcomes. Moreover, the condition that neutrinos had to have begun freely moving by the point of matter-radiation equality significantly limits the permissible parameter space, meaning even future $0 \nu \beta \beta$ decay experiments with a meV sensitivity to the effective neutrino mass would have difficulty detecting a signal.

Nonlocal gravity theory is a classical generalization of Einstein's gravity theory. This new approach involves the use of an integral operator to define the differential relationship between mass and gravity, and the connection between mass distribution and the resulting gravitational field. This description can also be expressed in terms of a nonlocal integral relationship, which the principle of correspondence applies to. This methodology extends the fundamental postulate of Einstein's theory and provides a basis for accounting for external influence on massive objects within their internal environments. The nonlocal approach results in the appearance of an additional integral term in the Poisson equation for the gravitational field, which can be solved using an integral transformation. This method enables the investigation of mass distribution effects on the gravitational field within internal environments and offers a framework for relating nonlocal effects to observable phenomena.

Understanding how genomic elements affect specific traits through genome-wide association studies remains complex due to the sheer number of available annotations. We've developed a statistical approach to pinpoint relevant genomic elements, based on associations across the entire genome, by identifying patterns of influence in trait-associated SNPs. This approach can incorporate multiple annotation types and has been successfully applied to eighteen human traits such as blood, platelet, hematocrit levels, height, macular degeneration and obesity, using data from one million SNPs. Our results show that certain patterns of association are repeatable across different studies and data sets for the same traits, and that they can be used to compare the effects of different genomic elements on traits even when study-specific effects vary significantly. Furthermore, we have found that certain annotation types that show repeated patterns of association across different studies may be subject to biases related to population sampling, and that results dependent on histone modification patterns can be used to infer the activity states of specific genomic elements.

This paper discusses recent findings from the LHC involving small systems studied
by the ALICE, ATLAS and CMS collaborations. Due to the growing significance
of QCD in small systems, particularly in situations with high multiplicity, not
all pertinent research can be covered within this report. It primarily examines
measurements focusing on collective behavior in small systems and new results on
strangeness enhancement observed in proton-proton interactions. It is essential to
note that many notable findings have been excluded from the discussion presented
here.

Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring X-ray bursts within short intervals. This study contradicts that idea by revealing that about half of the known LMXBs, featuring a neutron star as the primary component, exhibit outburst recurrence times exceeding a decade when detected by the MAXI telescope. Moreover, to reconcile the total population of neutron star binaries with observed and radio pulsar populations within the Milky Way, researchers find that a significant majority of these binaries have recurrence times exceeding a century for outbursts visible to the MAXI telescope and most remain undiscovered.

THz radiation enables the precise stimulation of vibrational frequencies in molecules and crystals, leading to the introduction of inertial influences on electrons. By drawing a comparison to classical mechanics, where circular motion generates Coriolis and centrifugal forces, analogous effects arise, specifically spin-rotation coupling, centrifugal field coupling, and the interplay of these forces with the spin-orbit interaction and the electron's distribution within an atom. These effects can persist for a few picoseconds following the initial stimulation, and potentially amplifying their magnitude could make this approach a promising means of controlling electronic states and chemical reactivity through vibration.

Improving neural conversational agents' ability to produce diverse, engaging responses in casual conversations is a challenge. To tackle this issue, this paper introduces two significant innovations. Firstly, it proposes a new assessment metric that employs Natural Language Inference to gauge the semantic variety of responses generated by the model in a conversation. Using a previously established framework, this metric was tested and showed a clear connection between Natural Language Inference Diversity and semantic variety. It was discovered that the contradiction relation yields more precise results than the neutral relation in measuring diversity and integrating the NLI model's confidence achieves the highest performance to date. Secondly, this paper demonstrates a way to modify the semantic variety metric, enabling it to function as a training objective to directly enhance the diversity of responses. When applied to several conversational generation tasks, this objective produced notable improvements in NLI Diversity, F-score.

The occurrence of sustainable hydrogen burning in very low-mass stars might be impacted by rotation due to the addition of centrifugal force and potential break-up caused by rapid spinning. Computer simulations model rotating low-mass stars with the capability for sustained nuclear reactions, considering a range of rotation rates, rather than slow rotation alone. Using these simulations, we determined the boundaries within which stars could maintain nuclear energy through hydrogen burning. These boundaries varied based on angular momentum. However, above a certain threshold (approximately 8.85 x 10^48 erg s) the boundaries broke into two distinct branches, resulting from objects losing mass and experiencing extreme spin. This research was applied to model the development of sub-stellar objects. Two possible scenarios were modeled: one with external forces gradually slowing the star, mainly controlled by spin-down time, and another where the star spins out of control, ultimately shedding mass and spinning down.

The technique of amplitude analysis in hadron decay studies is quite effective, 
However, this analysis faces a major challenge in addressing instrumental influences 
such as fluctuations in background levels and selection efficiency across different 
multidimensional kinematic scenarios.  This article will review traditional methods 
used for calculating efficiency and background probability and discuss the application 
of two techniques specifically density estimation using Gaussian processes and 
scalar functions density estimation aimed at mitigating the effects of instrumental 
rejections and background fluctuations in amplitude analyses.

A new model based on a comprehensive expression for radiation energy has been proposed, and it effectively elucidates the dynamics of afterglows in multiple contexts, including relativistic, non-relativistic phases and fireball radiations with radiative and adiabatic components.

Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number.

This paper will present our approach to optimizing bipedal robot walking assisted by thrusters using a closed-loop feedback system. We will focus on a bipedal robot model with a central torso and two legs, where the thrusters are attached to the legs and the feedback loop is created by measuring the displacement between planned and actual footstep locations. Our closed-loop control system ensures that the thrusters are adjusted in real-time to match the intended footstep pattern, thus preventing deviations caused by uneven terrain. Our simulation data shows that this closed-loop system can produce consistent walking results, even when the ground surface is uneven, with success rates of up to 90 percent for a wide range of obstacle sizes.

Becker-Denef-Lipschitz first observed in 1979 that over finite fields $k$, the total residue map $\text{res}$ from Laurent series to $k$ is expressible in a specific language, provided $t$ is included as a parameter. This discovery motivated further research into the properties of a specific mathematical theory related to valued fields. In the course of these investigations, the authors proved that this theory does not have a certain desirable feature and demonstrated that, for infinite fields $k$, the associated power series fields cannot be computationally decided. This, in turn, led to an analogous undecidability conclusion for a specific complex-valued field of power series.

In order to enhance side-channel attacks, this research introduces a new technique, HyperDegrade, which incorporates previous methods and employs simultaneous multithreading architectures.  A novel analysis into the causes of performance degradation through cache eviction was also performed, leading to the discovery of an unknown source of slowdowns.  Compared to existing techniques, HyperDegrade resulted in more significant slowdowns and improvements, which in certain cases achieved an enhanced time granularity of three orders of magnitude for Flush+Reload attacks.  Evaluations conducted across four different platforms, including Intel and AMD processors, validated the effectiveness of HyperDegrade.  Additionally, multiple approaches were proposed to optimize cache configuration for improved performance degradation, which was demonstrated to be cache-agnostic.  In relation to previous techniques, HyperDegrade exhibited improved scaling and a more significant boost from 2 to 64 threads.  The proposed technique is termed HyperDegrade Time Granularity Enhancement (HTGE), which includes two sub-techniques: HyperDegrade Array (HDArray) and HyperDegrade Tree (HDTree).  HTGE can be utilized for improving time granularity, which in turn may be utilized for improving cache eviction-based performance degradation, in addition to other side-channel attacks, such as Voltage Attack.  Ultimately, this research emphasizes the significance of considering cache behavior in the design of systems and microarchitectures, which is crucial for enhancing security against side-channel attacks.

A localized alteration in knot diagrams is referred to as an unknotting operation. It can be demonstrated that any knot diagram can be converted into a trivial unknot through a sequence of unknotting operations, combined with some variations in the diagram configuration, which are referred to as Reidemeister moves. Unknotting operations hold significant value in the field of knot theory; they serve a purpose in analyzing the intricacy of knots and knot-related properties. Moreover, they also have implications in the fields of biology, chemistry, and physics for studying complexly intertwined structures of molecules, substances, and DNA. The purpose of this paper was to introduce a novel type of unknotting operation, which is more precise and specialized compared to existing methods, such as the beta-move, by demonstrating that any knot diagram can be converted into a trivial unknot using a sequence of gamma-moves, combined with some variations in the diagram configuration, which are based on the classical Reidemeister moves.
We've demonstrated that combining the 1-cocycle of a long knot's space with Fox differential form results in a Vassiliev invariant of order three.

In cooperative systems with multiple agents, coordination enables tasks to be performed that would be beyond the capabilities of any single agent. We investigate the concept of coordination through strategic decision-making, focusing on a scenario where agents select between two tasks of varying difficulty that are randomly distributed and partially known. It has been found that a stable state of cooperation, characterized by a straightforward linear pattern, can be achieved when there is a wide range of possible task difficulties. Furthermore, it was discovered that the most advantageous action for each agent in response to an approachable strategy profile can be complex and nonlinear when the distribution of task difficulties is not uniform. A computational method has been established to calculate a cooperative equilibrium through learning within the set of linear policy options.

In this context, user devices serve as individual data providers in vertical FL, whereas in horizontal FL, they function as node computers that share aggregated data. To prevent information leakage, user devices in both methods employ encryption. Nonetheless, even with this protection, a critical security risk persists, where a third party can infer sensitive information from repeated exchanges of encrypted data. This phenomenon is known as a meta-information leak. To address this challenge, the researchers proposed an overlay network where data is securely shared among participants without revealing the origin of the data. Utilizing this framework, a new algorithm was developed to detect and remove residual metadata from shared data sets. Moreover, guidelines were provided for secure FL implementation, including selection of participants, data encryption, and a utility-based approach for inducing variability in shared data. The proposed solution was tested in multiple scenarios, including both synthetic and real-world data, to evaluate its effectiveness in preventing metadata leaks. The results showed an increase in utility up to 5 times when the overlay network was employed to remove residual metadata.

Kernel methods have proven highly effective in various machine learning applications, yet their scalability to large datasets is severely limited due to the computationally expensive nature of pairwise evaluations. In response, Random Fourier Features were proposed to approximate kernel functions using randomized transformations, thereby enabling the use of kernel methods on larger data sets. While widely adopted, this method has significant drawbacks, notably requiring an unnecessarily large number of features, directly proportional to the size of the dataset, in order to achieve satisfactory results comparable to traditional kernel-based methods. In order to circumvent these limitations and efficiently process large datasets, this paper introduces an alternative method of kernel approximation that leverages insights specific to the underlying data and offers both feature dimensionality reduction and performance enhancements. We test and evaluate this novel method against a range of competitors, including RFF, orthogonal random features, and the Nyström method.

In our study, we demonstrated how to modify and expand the concept of wreath products under different composition laws to accommodate various variations, including the standard method. Our comprehensive framework encompasses numerous well-known generalized wreath products, including dual wreath products, integral wreath products, and more. By shifting focus from specific examples to a broader perspective, our research provides a foundational understanding of these variations and their properties within our proposed framework. Ultimately, our work paves the way for further analysis of these generalized variations through the lens of our proposed framework.

This research paper examines conformally flat hypersurfaces of n-dimensional space (n is 4 or higher) within a hypersphere of n+2 dimensions. We start by classifying and describing these conformally flat hypersurfaces when they are compact and have a constant M\"obius curvature. To accomplish this, we utilize a complex representation of these hypersurfaces, specifically a holomorphic curve in a complex space of two dimensions that is equipped with a K\"ahlerian metric derived from the original hypersurface's curvature properties.

A new method of efficient wireless communication is proposed in a novel SWIPT system, enabling faster and more sustainable mobile data networks. The system, utilizing energy-harvesting technology from access points without the need for a splitter, allocates part of the frequency spectrum for information transmission and the remaining for energy capture. To analyze performance improvements, an optimization problem was created that maximizes energy gain and maintains a minimum data rate in a multi-user OFDMA network. Next, the model was refined to investigate throughput optimization in an SWIPT-enabled OFDMA system, resulting in a complex MINLP problem. Finally, an innovative harvesting technique based on a co-located receiver architecture and Generalized Antenna-Switching Technique was explored to improve the energy efficiency of SWIPT networks.

Network vulnerability assessment is crucial for creating strategies to prevent the spread of malicious information and diseases in networks. Researchers often study network immunization, but traditional approaches typically focus on broad measures, such as network criticality and component size. In contrast, this paper delves into a micro-level analysis, where the removal of individual nodes during an attack is examined in detail. Based on percolation theory, the authors analyze the effects of removing a single node that causes other nodes to disconnect from the main component. Specifically, this paper investigates the number of nodes that become disconnected from the main component as a result of removing one node. By applying this micro-level approach to a random attack on a Cayley tree network, the distribution of the resulting node removal sizes is derived.

The detection capabilities of advanced gravitational wave detectors are hindered in the high-frequency range by the quantum limitations of measurement and signal loss in optical recycling systems. Overcoming this constraint is critical for identifying gravitational waves generated by binary neutron star mergers. We present the concept of the sloshing Sagnac interferometer topology, an innovative variation of the Michelson design where the end mirrors are optically linked to form an additional resonating cavity. By transforming the detector into a system with multiple coupled cavities, this design outperforms the conventional signal-recycled Michelson setup by overcoming optical loss-induced limitations. Using advanced parameters similar to LIGO+, this new design offers improved sensitivity at high frequencies or better signal-to-noise ratios for specific binary neutron star merger waveforms, offering promising possibilities for future gravitational wave detectors.

Recent large-scale MIMO systems are considered an exciting development, capable of providing rapid data transfer in crowded environments. As a result of their substantial size, MIMO arrays are subject to space-based disruptions and varying ranges that affect how data is perceived by nearby devices. With a high number of devices often present in applications for these systems and the scarcity of pilot signals available for them, designing protocols and scheduling algorithms is increasingly complex. To address this challenge, a new joint protocol has been developed that leverages varying reception areas of devices for better access and prioritizes the scheduling of devices with distinct reception areas for more efficient signal sharing. According to the results obtained, this new scheme delivers significant gains over traditional approaches in terms of overall connectivity, reduces data transfer delays, and significantly boosts overall connectivity.

Recent observations at sub-millimeter/millimeter wavelengths have revealed that the morphological structure of young stars' surrounding disks comprise various shapes, including symmetrical patterns and features resembling spiral arms, and localized curved formations. Prior research primarily focused on modeling planetary interactions to explain observed patterns in disks. Although some exoplanets have been identified in such systems, many of these substructures emerge even before planetary formation as a result of gravitational interactions between multiple protoplanets and their surrounding disks. Numerical simulations of multiple protoplanet interactions within disks have been conducted in isolation or in specific configurations. Nonetheless, there is a lack of comprehensive modeling that accounts for various substructure formations observed in real-world systems. This work employs high-resolution, three-dimensional, radiative hydrodynamic simulations to model multiple protoplanet interactions within their surrounding disks, incorporating a wide range of mass scales from a few Earth masses to several Jupiter masses. The results of these simulations are compared with observed substructures and provide a framework for understanding the formation of visible patterns during the early stages of planetary development.

A question remains regarding the secondary component of GW190814 - whether it's a neutron star or a black hole of minimal mass. Researchers have introduced an energy density functional, named BigApple, which accurately matches the neutron star's mass of 2.60 solar masses and is in line with GW190814's data. By utilizing BigApple along with a coupling between the $\sigma$ and $\omega$ fields, a coupled $\sigma$-$\omega$ model is developed and compared to the existing coupled model based on the same parameter set. This comparison is made by transforming the effective masses of the particles. The resulting antiparticle charges of the $\sigma$ and $\omega$ fields, which were previously unknown, are also calculated. The BigApple parameter set also facilitates the prediction of the $\sigma$ and $\omega$ masses as well as their respective antiparticles. The properties of constant density quark states are also derived within the framework of the coupled model. The BigApple parameter set's ability to describe high-density quark states are examined by comparing the calculated energy densities to the ones obtained using the coupled model alone. The BigApple set's validity is further validated by correctly predicting the neutron star's radius and the f-mode frequency.

This research focuses on creating resilient Molmer-Sorensen gates using trapped ions arranged in a line, incorporating Gaussian amplitude modulation and a consistent laser frequency. We chose a frequency that maintains balanced entanglement accumulation across all motion modes to provide a significant degree of protection against frequency errors, particularly for long chains of ions. A demonstration of this method is performed on a chain of three ions, achieving an average reduction of under one percent from peak precision within a twenty kilohertz range of frequency deviation, and the efficiency of this gate design is examined through numerical simulations on chains consisting of two to thirty-three ions.

Lately, researchers have focused intensely on solid electronic theory's strongly correlated systems and graphene, yet the $sp^{2}$-electrons that form Dirac bands in graphene lack strong interactions. Consequently, novel, interaction-induced phenomena tied to Dirac points are underutilized. We propose GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$ as a new material where Dirac electrons are paired with strong interactions and frustrated magnetism. Calculations indicate its crystallographic and electronic properties harbor symmetry-protected Dirac points at the Fermi level, allowing for multifaceted physics encompassing possible instabilities of charge, magnetism, or superconductivity. By merging various methods to assess interaction effects, researchers have observed potential transitions to Mott-Hubbard, magnetic or charge ordering states, as well as $f$-wave unconventional superconductivity in this compound.

Researchers explored the capabilities of the NA62 experiment at CERN to enhance restrictions on a specific parameter in the Standard Model, specifically related to the interaction between a particular lepton and heavy neutral particles. By analyzing the process of $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$, they determined the present limit can be set at $2\times 10^{-6}$ for a particular lepton interaction with masses ranging from 125 to 144 MeV, with an optimal limit of $4\times 10^{-6}$ expected for optimal detection conditions and future data collections. This study also compares and contrasts methods of analyzing the $\pi^0$ decay products for optimizing lepton interaction limits with masses below 175 MeV.

Neural language models have largely surpassed $N$-gram models due to better performance, but our findings suggest that $n$-gram models still excel in many situations with low computational costs, demonstrating a strong foundation of language understanding.
