As a superconductor's expelled field generates a gradient near its surface, it induces a centripetal force that affects atomic motion within the interferometer, making it possible to measure this effect through atomic interference patterns. Based on the $10^{-12}$ g accuracy achieved in atomic gravity measurements, it's theoretically possible to measure expelled local magnetic field strengths at levels as precise as $10^{-14}$ Tesla.

In the case of a finite admixture model whose components and weights are unknown, techniques from stochastic convex geometry help us determine how the number of identifiable components changes in response to an increase in the amount of collected data. Additionally, placing a Dirichlet process prior on densities within a defined range enables us to recover a measure that narrows to the specific identifiable components, thereby yielding the corresponding admixture weights. A new algorithm is then proposed to accurately capture the complexity of data by utilizing only the minimum number of components necessary.

High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given class, utilizing distinct memory locations for each object.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory management system that automatically allocates memory for objects, reallocates memory when necessary, and efficiently shares memory across multiple threads.  To optimize memory access efficiency, DynaSOAr includes a thread block memory allocation algorithm that minimizes memory fragmentation and ensures each thread has a unique memory address for object variable access.  Our framework also provides a range of memory access optimization techniques, including a global memory access scheduler and a cache flush optimizer.  To facilitate easy migration of existing C++ code to GPU programming, DynaSOAr includes a wrapper class that converts standard C++ objects into SMMO objects.  Our experimental results using real-world applications and synthetic benchmarks demonstrated significant performance improvements over conventional multi-threaded GPU programming, with gains of up to 210 times.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for magnetic impurities, which can be experimentally validated via scanning tunneling microscopy. Utilizing the theoretical Nambu-Goldstone mode scenario, the model predicts the precise energy locations of the YSR states within the superconducting gap. This approach has been applied to the study of magnetic adatoms and monolayer magnetic metal islands on the clean and disordered surfaces of lead. Moreover, the model provides a clear understanding of the formation of bound states at the edges of magnetic nickel islands and offers predictions on the island edge state spectra. Additionally, the model has implications for the interpretation of magnetic phase diagrams of nickel islands and the theoretical analysis of inelastic tunneling spectroscopy.

The NASA $TESS$ mission's comprehensive sky survey allows the detection of rare, transiting planetary systems, particularly young planetary systems. By identifying and characterizing these systems, we can gain a deeper understanding of the evolution of young planets within their first billion years. We analyzed the planetary candidate inventory from the initial data release of the $TESS$ mission and developed a method to assess the ages of host stars by examining the characteristics of main sequence stars. We applied this approach to the $TESS$ discoveries and identified three candidates for planets orbiting young star systems. One of these systems, TOI-712, is particularly noteworthy, featuring a system similar to Jupiter's with a 455-d orbital period and a host star aged around 200-400 million years. Another system, TOI-1339, has a multi-planet system with orbits spanning from 5 to 500 days and a host star aged around 600-1100 million years. Both of these findings offer valuable insights into the evolution of young planets and their migration patterns.

We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2.  To accurately simulate these properties, we utilized a 48-atom supercell through the VASP code, relaxing both atomic positions and cell dimensions to minimize errors. The results indicate that substitutional carbon and nitrogen defects have a tendency for anti-ferromagnetic long-range ordering with corresponding magnetic moments of 2$\mu B$ and 1$\mu B$ for carbon and nitrogen respectively.  Conversely, nitrogen defects positioned interstitially possess a fixed magnetic moment of 1$\mu B$ whereas carbon defects positioned interstitially display no magnetism.  Moreover, calculations demonstrate that interstitial N defects lie at a saddle point in the total energy landscape, and that a more stable configuration is reached when these atoms bond with oxygen.  Notably, calculations also reveal that the energy difference between this more stable configuration and the interstitial N site lies within the range of high temperatures, suggesting that TiO2 containing N defects may exhibit both anti-ferromagnetic ordering and N-O bonding at elevated temperatures.

This letter describes the inspiration and an analytical method for detecting the production of top-quark pairs in the Large Hadron Collider through the identification of protons emitted at the front end. I demonstrate the feasibility of identifying the semi-leptonic production of top-quark pairs using a reduced dataset of 300 inverse picobarns of data. Additionally, I show that detecting fully-leptonic top-quark pair production is unlikely with this approach.

In 1993, Erdos and Galvin pioneered upper density problems within Ramsey theory, specifically the problem of identifying the highest $\lambda$ value such that in every two-edge coloring of the complete infinite graph, there exists an infinitely large, monochromatically colored subgraph resembling $F$ with an upper density of at least $\lambda$. We expand upon this research by providing a lower bound for this $\lambda$ value, with specific cases where the lower bound is equal to existing upper bounds for structures like cliques and odd cycles, and a $1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}$ value for triangles that surpasses the former record of 3/5.

Our analysis highlights the benefits of using qudits instead of qubits in scalar Quantum Electrodynamics in $(1+1)$d, specifically regarding their tolerance to errors. When measuring the mass gap using an out-of-time correlator as noise increases from both amplitude damping and Pauli channels, our findings reveal that simulations utilizing qutrits can handle up to 10 to 100 times more gate noise than their qubit-based counterparts for the same mass determination error. Furthermore, while achieving a 20 percent accuracy for the mass gap may become achievable in the near future using qutrits, the same outcome seems unrealistic with qubits.

Research indicates that positrons are efficiently produced through interactions between intense lasers and solid materials, specifically within the context of strong-field quantum electrodynamics. However, the polarization properties of these positrons remain unknown, hindering potential uses. Our simulations, which account for the interaction of photons with strong electric fields in solids, reveal that the polarization of generated positrons can be significant, potentially exceeding 50%. Factors contributing to polarization, including the angle between the target surface and the incoming laser beam, the duration of the interaction, and the production mechanism of positrons, were identified through in-depth analysis.

Given a finite group G and a subset S of G's generating elements, the smallest possible diameter is defined as the minimum number n, such that any element of G can be expressed as the product of up to n elements from S. This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that scales polynomially for a fixed-sized generating set, and it demonstrates that these groups have a significant abelian subgroup close to their highest order, making up a substantial fraction of the group's total size. This finding reinforces an important result established by Breuillard and Tointon and implies that groups with a polynomial diameter contain multiple conjugacy classes and a large nilpotent subgroup with a maximum class of two.

This paper presents a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling real-time thermal monitoring in systems that employ dynamic voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which are then converted into digital data by an analog-to-digital converter. The design incorporates a unique frequency selection method that allows for a high-resolution temperature reading within a limited time frame, making it suitable for use in systems that require frequent temperature readings. The temperature sensor was fabricated using a 180nm CMOS process and features a compact footprint of 0.021mm^2. Experimental results reveal a temperature reading accuracy of 3.2°C for a 10-minute period and a conversion time of 20ms for a 16-bit digital output.

This PhD research focuses on exploring specific geometric constructs over Lie groupoids and differential stacks. Building on the foundations laid out in [arXiv:2103.04560, arXiv:2012.08447, arXiv:2012.08442, arXiv:1907.00375], the study establishes connections between key concepts within this framework. Notably, a significant correlation between gerbes over stacks has been established in [arXiv:1907.00375], the development of the Chern-Weil map for principal bundles over Lie groupoids equipped with a connection has been introduced in [arXiv:2012.08447], the relationship between connections on principal bundles over Lie groupoids and gerbe descent data has been defined in [arXiv:2012.08442], and topological 2-cocycles over topological stacks have been linked to line bundles over line bundles over the stack in [arXiv:2103.04560].

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, which are more substantial than typical starless or protostellar cores, of approximately 24 to 28 solar masses. Unlike the cores without outflows, these cores, which are linked to prestellar cores, have masses greater than necessary to form a low-mass star and have a slower formation rate. It is proposed that these cores, which are more significant than expected, may indicate a transition stage of low-mass starless cores that have not yet begun to evolve and could provide valuable insights into the initial stages of low-mass, dense core evolution.

Positive definite functions on the sphere are crucial in various applications, particularly in signal processing and harmonic analysis. A widely utilized and versatile class of such functions is the set of mean-square continuous functions, defined as linear combinations of the eigenfunctions of the Dirac operator on the sphere. The framework of this paper delves into the analysis of a specific class of mean-square continuous functions, characterized by their expansion in Gegenbauer polynomials. The primary objective of this study is to establish an explicit condition for positive definiteness of a zonal function on the sphere. The proposed condition leverages the derivatives of the Gegenbauer polynomials and their corresponding coefficients in the expansion. The key aspect of this requirement is its specificity to the Gegenbauer setting, as it supersedes a more general positive definiteness criterion already established for this context. The connection between the proposed condition and the well-known result from the Gegenbauer expansion framework is demonstrated. The applicability and utility of this condition are illustrated through specific examples of the radial part of spherical harmonics and the eigenfunctions of the Dirac operator on the sphere.

The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements has been validated by comparing them with existing models. Furthermore, we extracted the stick-slip process's characteristic parameters from our data. These results will contribute to the development of surface roughness-induced stick-slip models and provide valuable data for stress measurements in the laboratory.

This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the challenge, we employed a multi-classifier ensemble consisting of 13 convolutional neural networks (CNN), and devised two methods to handle the outlier class. Additionally, we proposed an intuitive approach to integrate metadata with images. Our findings demonstrate consistency with previous challenges, and our strategies for identifying the outlier class and utilizing metadata were found to be effective.

The steady-state behavior of an elastic membrane, situated between two fluids of differing densities in a rotating Hele-Shaw cell, subject to external pressure, is examined in a study that also compares its inextensibility to that of an extremely elastic membrane. When the inner fluid density surpasses the outer fluid density, the membrane exhibits a Rayleigh-Taylor-like instability caused by centrifugal force, competing with the curvature and tension-driven restorative forces, thus dictating the size of the developed finger. Numerical computation techniques are utilized to analyze not just nonlinear finger patterns but also modes of sausagelike deformities that can occur when the membrane's elasticity is not extremely high. The associated governing equations can also be solved analyically to determine the linear stability of both sausagelike deformities and the state of equilibrium. The results show that sausagelike deformities will eventually grow from even very small initial disturbances, in contrast to the experience of the nonrotating, two-dimensional case. The size of the sausagelike deformities also increases over time and is determined by the ratio of the viscosity of the inner fluid to the inner fluid density, as well as the rate of spin, the membrane's elasticity, and the applied pressure. The onset of the sausagelike state can be identified by examining the rate of growth of small initial sinusoidal perturbations applied to the membrane.

Scientists have identified the presence of two specific isomers, 1- and 2-ethynyl-1,3-cyclopentadiene, of ethynyl cyclopentadiene, within a interstellar medium. This discovery makes it the second instance where this molecule has been detected in space and raises the detection levels to 1.5 times the previous amount, with estimated column densities of 1.5 x 10^13 particles per square meter for both isomers. Additionally, a weaker indication of ethynyl benzene was observed with a column density likely exceeding five times that of the cyclopentadiene isomers. This discovery was made possible through the analysis of data collected from two specific observations made towards the Taurus Molecular Cloud at a wavelength of 4.75 meters. The findings were consistent with models suggesting the particles reside within a very dense gas region.

In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks.

The significant discrepancy between advancing computational technology and real-world problem-solving led to a new field of study. Abramson and Parashar suggest that a parallel disparity in complex software and challenging practical applications calls for the emergence of translational computer science. From this viewpoint, we reexamine the development and implementation of grid computing. A translational perspective is helpful for comprehending the progress of grid computing technology. Specifically, we show how developing the grid computing infrastructure and the Globus Toolkit thrived due to a focus on applying research directly. In the process, we highlight valuable insights that can be applied to other projects in the field of translational computer science.

A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines adiabatic and bulk viscous components. This model has the ability to smoothly transition between the equations of state for dark energy and dust at different cosmological epochs, by asymptotically interpolating between two power laws. A constant viscosity coefficient underlies the model's dissipative component. Using a phase space analysis, we investigate the model's dynamics in a framework that is robust and solution-independent. Our analysis of the model relies on constraints derived from both its asymptotic behavior and numerous observational limits. Through numerical computations, we solve the Hubble parameter equation, which yields results when plotted against a set of current observations. Our findings indicate that the model is capable of describing the evolution of the universe during various stages, from its initial state to the present day. Moreover, we determine that the model can bridge the periods of deceleration and acceleration in the universe's evolution, even as it adheres to both the asymptotic behavior of $\Omega_{DE}(a)$ and the current value of the Hubble constant.

Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting likelihood fits for individual neutrino and dark matter operators with varying Lorentz structures and photon spectrums. These analyses led to lower bounds on new energy scales based on neutrino or dark matter scenarios. Specifically, the most stringent limits on energy scales were found to be 12.8 GeV for neutrinos and 11.6 GeV for dark matter within their respective effective field theories. We also found that J/ψ decay into purely invisible matter imposes additional constraints on certain effective operators, with energy scales above 100 GeV for dipole operators. Moreover, our analysis revealed that J/ψ invisible decays can be sensitive to light dark matter mass ranges inaccessible to direct detection experiments, with future facilities such as the Super Tau Charm Factory having the potential to significantly lower these limits by two orders of magnitude.

This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across various dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). We offer a comprehensive framework consisting of the theoretical underpinnings and a step-by-step implementation guide for the algorithm. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of MFSSA through comparative studies of reconstruction accuracy in multivariate functional time series (MFTS) and real-world applications, including the analysis of temperature curves and heart rate signals. Additionally, MFSSA is made available through the Rfssa R package for user convenience.

The power law decay $p(t,x) \sim t^{-\phi(x,b)/2}$ holds, where $p(t,x)$ is the probability that, during the interval $[1,t]$, the random walk $S$ with zero-mean increments has spent a fraction of time greater than $x$ with non-negative values, occurring for a walk that is defined by finitely many i.i.d. increment values. The parameter $\phi(x,b)$ is determined by the probability $\mathbb{P}(\text{L\'evy}(1/2,\kappa(x,b))<0)$ where $\kappa(x,b) = \frac{\sqrt{1-x}b-\sqrt{1+x}}{\sqrt{1-x}b+\sqrt{1+x}}$ with $b = b_S \geq 0$ indicating the relative magnitude between positive and negative excursions of the random walk.

The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and features a helical antenna to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode of discharge. Until now, it was unclear if this plasma source could achieve helicon mode, which is essential for it to function effectively. A study was conducted to verify this capability, involving detailed measurements of plasma parameters and particle energy spectra. It also included analysis of plasma source dynamics using a computer simulation. The results show that plasma in the source reaches the helicon state, confirming it is suitable for the IShTAR experiment. Additionally, it was possible to determine the plasma source's operating limits and explain measured plasma parameters using computer simulations.

While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with one another, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which involves marking cell centers rather than outlining individual cells. However, current point-based nucleus segmentation models require a dense set of annotations, which is time-consuming to obtain manually. To make cancer diagnosis more efficient, researchers have been proposing methods to annotate cells as "foreground" or "background" without specifying their location. In response to these developments, the research community has begun to evaluate point-based nucleus segmentation models based on mask annotations. To facilitate this evaluation, the authors have created two new datasets with mask annotations, CPM-pan and CPM-breast, which contain pancreatic and breast cancer images respectively. To support efficient training and evaluation, the data format has been standardized as a binary mask, where the center of each cell is marked as '1' and the background is marked as '0'. The resulting datasets can be used to evaluate point-based nucleus segmentation models, including the use of recall measures that prioritize the detection of individual cells.

Let's consider a non-Archimedean local field of characteristic not two and denote it by F. Additionally, let G be either a specific type of special orthogonal group with an odd number of dimensions or a symplectic group with a specific dimensionality, denoted as SO(2r+1)(F) or Sp(2r)(F) respectively. This paper intends to establish the local converse theorem for the representation of G. To this end, for two given irreducible admissible generic representations of G, with shared central character and gamma factors, our result stipulates that these representations are isomorphic. To prove this, we need to establish the isomorphism between the representations, hence our strategy involves several key steps: first, we can reduce the problem to a more manageable case where the central character is trivial; second, we can further reduce the problem to a case where the gamma factors of the representations are equal; third, we can then reduce the problem to a case where the supercuspidal components of the representations have a specific property; fourth, we can then establish the isomorphism between the representations whose supercuspidal components have this specific property.

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements, such as those found in recurrent and convolutional networks. Additionally, we show that GCNNs can be viewed as a series of successive feature extraction processes, where each stage identifies more refined patterns of the input data.

In a three-dimensional spacetime, Einstein's gravity theory can be accurately emulated by a covariant, three-dimensional f(R) gravity theory when the scalar field exhibits certain behavior, specifically by displaying a bounded, single-hump configuration as it relates to the metric's variation. The associated action must result in a first-order term in the metric and a second-order term in the scalar field, along with the condition that the field's holonomy is zero. The approach involves a consistent expansion of the metric and scalar field around their stable, solution configurations. As a result, the resulting three-dimensional gravity theory can be formulated using the Palatinus-Pomeransky-Wisniewski (PPW) potential, which, in turn, enables the determination of metric values for given scalar field configurations. The proposed method can be applied to both bosonic and fermionic fields. The obtained three-dimensional gravity theory exhibits the same holonomy properties as its original, four-dimensional counterpart. The approach also yields the solution to the three-dimensional soliton system along with the geodesic equations that define its dynamics.

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Synthetic Aperture (SA) ultrasound imaging has been employed for elastography, yet its limited angular sampling results in orientation ambiguity and image rotation, thereby complicating the direction estimation during deformation. To overcome this limitation, researchers have proposed the Virtual Source Synthetic Aperture (VSSA) method that uses a virtual source array equivalent to the real receiver array to facilitate wide-angle SA imaging. This approach enables the estimation of lamda (lambda) and mu (mu) tissue parameters with higher precision. Additionally, the increased angular sampling reduces rotation-induced image misalignment during elastography, simplifying direction estimation and deformation detection. Experimental evaluations using tissue-mimicking phantoms demonstrated the superior performance of VSSA over traditional SA. The study highlights the VSSA method's capacity to enhance SA elastography, thereby improving the accuracy of tissue property characterization.

Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as distinct yet related concepts. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an expanded framework, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in natural deduction, ensuring correctness and safety in accordance with the original specifications. This approach can be seen as a natural extension to the concept of a computability logic web, but now incorporating the capacity for forward reasoning.

In the context of dynamic data streams, where Euclidean space points are added or removed from a dataset, we develop a one-pass coreset algorithm for solving the $k$-means clustering problem. Our solution employs storage capacity of approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$, making it the first algorithm for this problem to utilize dimension-dependent storage while maintaining linear dependence on the target center count $k$.

We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games by subdividing the environment into manageable segments. This approach splits decision-making into two levels: a higher layer that allocates agents to geospatial partitions, and a lower layer handling movements within those areas. To execute this strategy, we develop a computational framework comprising three stages: (1) predicting future partition assignments, (2) calculating risk in specified areas, and (3) resolving agent movements. Through simulations of various scenarios, our hierarchical model demonstrates performance enhancements, particularly in reducing the time required to solve large-scale PEGs.

Due to the tendency for high-energy lepton colliders to radiate forward and resemble weak boson colliders beyond a few TeV, a new perspective is taken that treats weak bosons as fundamental constituents of atoms, analogous to electrons. Within this context, a new potential phenomenon is pointed out: atoms made of heavy weak bosons can break apart into a forward and a backward jet, exhibiting a similar pattern to the dual parton model observed in proton collisions. Similar challenges and opportunities arise in identifying this process, which could result in heavy Higgs particle production through a mechanism known as "neutrino dark matter." As a result, a search for a heavy Higgs boson in the $b\bar b \mu^+\mu^-$ final state at future lepton colliders is proposed, with the potential to complement existing strong production searches and to reveal the presence of neutrino dark matter even if it remains elusive in traditional searches.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios.

We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma from 1931, and a corollary that formal systems cannot be both complete and consistent when using first-order logic.

This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we prove that if u meets these requirements in three dimensions, then there exists a constant C, independent of λ, such that |u| is bounded by C|λ|^(1/3) near any point.

In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes, represented by the posterior distribution. We developed a method to generate a multitude of high-quality samples per second from the posterior distribution by using a regularized conditional Wasserstein space, which outperformed current methods according to Fr\'{e}chet inception distance metrics in applications like MRI with multiple coils and image inpainting.

This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions for specific invariant configurations in polynomial systems and fractional-order systems. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in planar systems and the conditions under which linear subspaces remain invariant in fractional-order systems. We also discuss a notable result highlighting that in fractional-order systems, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant manifolds.

The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several months. Analysis of these screens yields their locations, sizes, Doppler shifts, and velocities. Only one velocity was found to be abnormal, suggesting that the velocities of screens in the line of sight to PSR B1133+16 are generally consistent with random distributions, in contrast to sources observed towards other pulsars. Infrared archival data from Spitzer reveal a massive AGB star and a reddened dark cloud within the same field of view as the pulsar, likely being the screens' origin; however more data is needed to confirm this hypothesis.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's performance in speech synthesis.

The theory of shadows provides an axiomatic framework for certain mathematical structures that underlie geometric constructions. Initially developed to model vector bundles and similar constructs, the theory has been expanded to encompass a broader category of morphisms preserving properties, which it terms 'arrows.' These arrows exhibit morita invariance, meaning their behavior remains consistent across equivalent category constructions. A notable aspect of the theory of shadows is its ability to define constructions without relying on set theory. The underlying idea is to describe the elements of a set using descriptive set theory, ensuring the absence of implicit set theoretic assumptions. The associated proof demonstrates that the theory of shadows maintains its morita invariance characteristics without depending on specific category constructions.

Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically extracts challenging samples and incorporates them into a contrastive learning framework. Our algorithm can be used for both supervised and unsupervised sound source localization. We tested our approach on two real-world datasets and found it outperformed the current state-of-the-art methods by a substantial margin. Our code is available online at: https://github.com/ghali95/SISL.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Research has demonstrated the potential benefits of representing graphs within hyperbolic geometry, which is better suited for detecting hierarchical relationships. In line with this concept, we propose a hyperbolic graph convolutional network (HGCN). The proposed framework maps points onto the surface of a hyperbolic sphere and employs the geodesic distance metric in network calculations. We also introduce a method to dynamically update the hyperbolic embedding of nodes based on node importance. The framework and the embedding method can be used separately. The proposed framework can be viewed as a variation of the original GCN, and our experiments have shown that this variant performs better. We have tested the framework and methods across five different datasets and the source code is publicly available. Experimental results have shown consistent performance improvements over the original GCN and complex network convolutional network (CNCN).

This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability inequality and a compactness-uniqueness argument. An operator theoretical approach provides the regularity needed for initial conditions, thereby obtaining the desired stability estimate.

We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating
variations in impulsivity, which is analogous to the 2007 Tsallis delay discounting
model proposed by Takahashi, with a dual parameter model for added flexibility.
We demonstrate that our model, in contrast to the popular hyperbolic delay
discounting model, does not confuse discount rate with the impulsivity parameter,
thus providing a clear distinction between these key concepts. Additionally,
our model surpasses the Tsallis delay discounting model in terms of explanatory
power regarding human economic behavior, according to an ordinal regression
analysis.

When considering linearized gravity within a harmonic gauge theory for a symmetric tensor field, implementing the harmonic gauge yields multiple gauge options, resulting in the gauge appearing as a class rather than a singular choice.  This feature provides a physical justification for adopting a specific covariant harmonic gauge that arises when a mass term is added to the gravitational perturbation.  Specifically, one particular choice of harmonic gauge leads to a linearized massive gravity model with the correct five degrees of freedom and avoids the vDVZ discontinuity, in contrast to the standard Fierz-Pauli theory.

For a class of quadratic Hamiltonians, a transformation of the Hamiltonian H into the canonical form H' in terms of creation and annihilation operators A^† and A is demonstrated, with A and A^† expressed in terms of the original operators J and K. The thermodynamic properties of a state in thermal equilibrium with respect to H are shown to be determined by a thermal matrix T, whose properties the state satisfies. The structure of T is revealed to be composed of submatrices defined by the Weyl symbol of thermal expectation values of products of J, K, A, and A^†. The canonical form of the Hamiltonian H' is then utilized to establish that the thermal matrix T can be expressed in a diagonal form, with the submatrices defined by the eigenvalues of the thermal matrix. The implications of this new perspective on the thermal equilibrium states are discussed.

The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to illustrate negative temperature through both mathematical and graphical means, specifically in the context of a two-level system. We contend that the simplicity of these calculations can offer undergraduates a clear, tangible understanding of the concept of negative absolute temperature.

Within the simplest scoto-seesaw model, we examine the consistency between the electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino characteristics, and dark matter behavior. By integrating the minimal dark sector into the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw framework, we establish a comprehensive understanding of the neutrino oscillation length spectrum. Here, the atmospheric and solar mass scales are directly related, with $\theta_{23}$ maximally mixed and the solar mixing angle $\theta_{11}$ determined by $\theta_{12}$ and $\tan\beta$. Furthermore, we determine the valid parameter ranges for the atmospheric and solar mass scales, the dark sector coupling, and the neutrino dark matter candidate masses. Additionally, we investigate the dark matter relic abundance and determine the constraints on the neutrino oscillation length spectrum. Utilizing the most recent atmospheric neutrino data and the tau damping tail anomaly, we establish the potential for future experiments to detect the predicted signals.

We employ exact diagonalization to examine the effects of spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions on the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ $d$-orbital states in a cubic crystal structure, characteristic of transition metal oxides. By directly comparing with $t_{2g}$ only or $e_g$ only models based on electron filling, we investigate the magnetic properties of all possible $d$-shell configurations, incorporating calculations of the total magnetic moment, orbital occupation, and effective spin-orbit coupling. The resulting parameters are expressed in terms of interaction strength, spin-orbit coupling, and crystal field splitting within relevant 4d and 5d transition metal oxide ranges. Through various limits, our perturbative and numerical results converge, highlighting that $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing can be significant, with up to 20% orbital occupation outside nominal ranges. These findings hold important implications for experimental interpretation and can influence the theoretical models used to analyze magnetic properties and phases in these materials.

This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through analytical means. Furthermore, it explores connections between these results and the related mathematical theories of extremal transitions and FJRW.

Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produces authentic chest X-rays. By incorporating an encoder from the Cyclic Reverse Generator framework, we successfully developed an inverse mapping system to recreate synthetic X-rays accurately and reconstruct organs on real X-rays. By fine-tuning latent codes, we successfully transplanted a cardiac enlargement condition onto normal chest X-rays. Our research was showcased at the Medical Imaging meets NeurIPS Workshop 2020, a satellite event of the 34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems held in Vancouver, Canada.

ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and
advanced analysis. It is capable of handling object-feature tables that include
numerical values and text-based labels for objects and features. The tool
encompasses several statistical techniques such as weighted PCA, elastic maps,
linear discriminant analysis, and decision tree construction, in addition to
K-Means clustering and multilinear regression. With customizable visualizations
and an interactive 3D viewer, ViDaExpert enables the creation of 3D scenes
from data and facilitates rapid, in-depth analysis of data, encompassing
elementary to complex methodologies.
